name: Chamomile
description:
Chamomile here is German chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla, also filed as M. recutita), whose dried flower heads are brewed as a calming tea. One of its flavones, apigenin, binds the benzodiazepine site in vitro and has its own entry; how much of chamomile's effect apigenin accounts for is not known, and an extract standardized to other constituents may give different results.

The controlled evidence comes from a few small trials of extract capsules. In 57 people with mild to moderate generalized anxiety disorder, an extract standardized to 1.2% apigenin, taken at 220–1,100 mg a day for eight weeks, lowered anxiety scores more than placebo, a modest difference (P = 0.047). In a longer study, people who responded to 12 weeks of 1,500 mg a day were switched to either chamomile or placebo for 26 weeks; fewer relapsed on chamomile (15% against 26%), but the difference was not significant. In 34 adults with chronic insomnia, 270 mg twice a day for four weeks did not change sleep-diary measures compared with placebo.

One case report describes multiple internal hemorrhages in a woman taking warfarin after she used chamomile tea and lotion.
